newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada claims success in inflation fight.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada claims success in inflation fight.

text.p: Low inflation, more than any other economic trend, was the key factor in the easing of monetary conditions in the Canadian economy last year, said the Bank of Canada in its annual report for 1996.

The report, presented in Canada's parliament on Thursday, said the bank's successful battle to keep inflation in a target range of 1.0-3.0 percent allowed interest rates to drift down to levels not seen since the 1960s.
Canadian inflation, measured by the total consumer price index (CPI), rose by 2.2 percent in 1996. The core CPI, which excludes food and energy prices, climbed 1.8 percent last year.

The Bank has cut its key bank rate by a total of 500 basis points since the middle of 1995. The bank rate, currently 3.25 percent, is the top of the central bank's target range for overnight lending to financial institutions.
The Bank also attributed the decline of interest rates to the federal government's deficit-reduction strategy and Canada's improving balance of payments.

Canada's Finance Minister Paul Martin revealed last month that Canada's budget deficit was C$19 billion (US$13.9 billion) in fiscal 1996-97, more than C$5 billion (US$3.7 billion) lower than initially projected.
"These developments reflect a much higher level of confidence in the value of our money on the part of both Canadian and foreign investors," the Bank said.
